title: The Children of Kauai
text:
In 1955, the psychologist Emmy Werner and her colleagues began a study of every child born that year on the Hawaiian island of Kauai, 698 in all. Most came from families of plantation workers of Japanese, Filipino, Hawaiian and other backgrounds. The researchers gathered information from before birth and then followed the children at ages one, two, ten and eighteen, and later into adulthood.

About a third of the children were considered at high risk. They had been born after a difficult pregnancy or birth and grew up in poverty, often with family conflict, divorce, or a parent with alcoholism or mental illness. Most of these children did develop serious learning or behavior problems by their teens.

But about one in three of the high-risk children did not. By eighteen they had grown into competent, caring young adults. Werner and Ruth Smith looked closely at what set them apart. These children tended to have easygoing temperaments that drew people to them. Above all, almost every one of them had at least one person who offered steady care and attention: a parent, a grandparent, an older sibling, an aunt, a teacher, or a neighbor.

Werner and Smith described the findings in the book Vulnerable but Invincible, and the study became a foundation of resilience research.
lesson: A single caring adult can change the course of a child's life. You may be that person for a child who is not your own.
source: Werner, E. E., and Smith, R. S. (1982). Vulnerable but Invincible: A Longitudinal Study of Resilient Children and Youth. New York: McGraw-Hill.
